references.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, et al.
references.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial.
references.finding: Over 4.5 years, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen users showed no detectable increase in skin aging and 24% less photoaging than discretionary users (relative odds 0.76, 95% CI 0.59-0.98); 30 mg/day beta-carotene had no overall effect.

references.authors: Green AC, Williams GM, Logan V, et al.
references.title: Reduced melanoma after regular sunscreen use: randomized trial follow-up.
references.finding: Ten years after the 4.5-year Nambour trial ended, 11 primary melanomas occurred in the daily-sunscreen group vs 22 in the discretionary group (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.24-1.02, P=0.051); invasive melanomas 3 vs 11 (HR 0.27).

references.authors: Green A, Williams G, Neale R, et al.
references.title: Daily sunscreen application and betacarotene supplementation in prevention of basal-cell and squamous-cell carcinomas of the skin: a randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: Daily SPF 15+ sunscreen for 4.5 years did not change the number of people developing basal- or squamous-cell carcinoma, but cut the number of squamous-cell tumours by 39% (rate ratio 0.61); 30 mg/day beta-carotene had no effect on either cancer.

references.authors: Fisher GJ, Wang ZQ, Datta SC, et al.
references.title: Pathophysiology of premature skin aging induced by ultraviolet light.
references.finding: A single UV exposure induced collagenase, gelatinase and stromelysin in human skin and raised collagen breakdown by 58%; repeated exposures kept MMP activity elevated for 7 days, and tretinoin pretreatment blocked MMP induction by 70-80%.

references.authors: Mouret S, Baudouin C, Charveron M, et al.
references.title: Cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers are predominant DNA lesions in whole human skin exposed to UVA radiation.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: In whole human skin, UVA produced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers in larger amounts than the oxidative lesion 8-oxo-dG, and UVA-induced dimers were repaired more slowly than UVB-induced ones; skin protected keratinocytes well against UVB but weakly against UVA.

references.authors: Liebel F, Kaur S, Ruvolo E, et al.
references.title: Irradiation of skin with visible light induces reactive oxygen species and matrix-degrading enzymes.
references.finding: Visible light (400-700 nm) induced ROS, pro-inflammatory cytokines and MMP-1 in skin equivalents and free-radical activity in human skin; standard UVA/UVB sunscreens barely reduced this, while a sunscreen with an antioxidant combination did (Johnson & Johnson authors).

references.authors: Diffey B, Cadars B
references.title: An appraisal of the need for infrared radiation protection in sunscreens.
references.finding: Annual solar IR-A doses are comparable to those of furnace workers who show little chronic skin damage, so there is no compelling evidence that solar IR causes observable skin harm and IR-protection claims in sunscreens are premature.

references.authors: Schroeder P, Lademann J, Darvin ME, et al.
references.title: Infrared radiation-induced matrix metalloproteinase in human skin: implications for protection.
references.finding: Physiological doses of near-infrared (IR-A) raised dermal MMP-1 in 80% of people and lowered skin antioxidant content; topical antioxidants prevented the MMP-1 rise, a mitochondrial ROS-mediated response.

references.authors: Grether-Beck S, Marini A, Jaenicke T, et al.
references.title: Effective photoprotection of human skin against infrared A radiation by topically applied antioxidants: results from a vehicle controlled, double-blind, randomized study.
references.finding: SPF 30 sunscreen plus an antioxidant cocktail (grape seed extract, vitamin E, ubiquinone, vitamin C) reduced IR-A-induced MMP-1 in human skin, whereas the same sunscreen alone did not; the outcome was a molecular marker, not visible aging.

references.authors: Castanedo-Cazares JP, Hernandez-Blanco D, Carlos-Ortega B, et al.
references.title: Near-visible light and UV photoprotection in the treatment of melasma: a double-blind randomized trial.
references.finding: Adding iron oxide (visible-light-blocking) to an SPF 50+ sunscreen improved melasma severity scores by 15% and colorimetry by 28% more than UV-only sunscreen over 8 weeks with hydroquinone.

references.authors: Pinnell SR, Yang H, Omar M, et al.
references.title: Topical L-ascorbic acid: percutaneous absorption studies.
references.finding: In pig skin, L-ascorbic acid only penetrated when formulated at pH below 3.5, absorption peaked at 20% concentration, tissue levels saturated after 3 daily applications with a ~4-day half-life, and common derivatives did not raise skin vitamin C.

references.authors: Humbert PG, Haftek M, Creidi P, et al.
references.title: Topical ascorbic acid on photoaged skin. Clinical, topographical and ultrastructural evaluation: double-blind study vs. placebo.
references.finding: In a 6-month double-blind trial, 5% vitamin C cream improved clinical global scores, skin microrelief and deep furrows versus its vehicle, with ultrastructural evidence of elastic-tissue repair.

references.authors: Correia G, Magina S
references.title: Efficacy of topical vitamin C in melasma and photoaging: A systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review of randomized trials: topical vitamin C smoothed wrinkled skin and lightened pigmentation, but all studies were small and long-term use may be needed for visible change.

references.authors: De Dormael R, Bastien P, Sextius P, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C Prevents Ultraviolet-induced Pigmentation in Healthy Volunteers: Bayesian Meta-analysis Results from 31 Randomized Controlled versus Vehicle Clinical Studies.
references.finding: A Bayesian pooling of 31 intra-individual vehicle-controlled studies run by L'Oreal found topical vitamin C reduced UV-induced pigmentation dose-dependently but did not speed depigmentation afterwards.

references.authors: Lin FH, Lin JY, Gupta RD, et al.
references.title: Ferulic acid stabilizes a solution of vitamins C and E and doubles its photoprotection of skin.
references.finding: Adding ferulic acid to 15% L-ascorbic acid plus 1% alpha-tocopherol improved the solution's chemical stability and doubled its photoprotection of (pig) skin from about 4-fold to about 8-fold, also reducing thymine dimers.

references.authors: Lin JY, Selim MA, Shea CR, et al.
references.title: UV photoprotection by combination topical antioxidants vitamin C and vitamin E.
references.finding: In pig skin, 15% L-ascorbic acid plus 1% alpha-tocopherol applied for 4 days gave a 4-fold protection against UV erythema and sunburn cells, better than either vitamin alone, and reduced thymine dimers.

references.authors: Chen AC, Martin AJ, Choy B, et al.
references.title: A Phase 3 Randomized Trial of Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention.
references.finding: ONTRAC: nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months cut new non-melanoma skin cancers by 23% (95% CI 4-38) and actinic keratoses by 11-20% versus placebo; there was no benefit after stopping.

references.authors: Allen NC, Martin AJ, Snaidr VA, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide for Skin-Cancer Chemoprevention in Transplant Recipients.
references.finding: ONTRANS: in immunosuppressed transplant recipients, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily for 12 months did not reduce keratinocyte cancers (207 vs 210; rate ratio 1.0); the trial stopped early for poor recruitment.

references.authors: Breglio KF, Knox KM, Hwang J, et al.
references.title: Nicotinamide for Skin Cancer Chemoprevention.
references.finding: In Veterans Affairs records, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily was associated with 14% lower skin-cancer risk overall and 54% lower risk when started after a first skin cancer; no overall reduction was seen in transplant recipients.

references.authors: Mainville L, Smilga AS, Fortin PR
references.title: Effect of Nicotinamide in Skin Cancer and Actinic Keratoses Chemoprophylaxis, and Adverse Effects Related to Nicotinamide: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Nicotinamide halved skin cancers versus control (rate ratio 0.50, 0.29-0.85; 5 trials, 552 patients), with heterogeneity explained by risk of bias, and slightly increased digestive adverse effects.

references.authors: Bissett DL, Oblong JE, Berge CA
references.title: Niacinamide: A B vitamin that improves aging facial skin appearance.
references.finding: Procter & Gamble split-face trial: 5% topical niacinamide twice daily for 12 weeks reduced fine lines, hyperpigmented spots, red blotchiness and sallowness and improved elasticity versus vehicle.

references.authors: Weiss JS, Ellis CN, Headington JT, et al.
references.title: Topical tretinoin improves photoaged skin. A double-blind vehicle-controlled study.
references.finding: Tretinoin cream improved photoaging on all treated forearms and 14 of 15 treated faces over 16 weeks, versus no improvement on vehicle-treated faces; irritation was the main side effect.

references.authors: Kafi R, Kwak HS, Schumacher WE, et al.
references.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol).
references.finding: 0.4% retinol applied up to 3 times weekly for 24 weeks reduced fine wrinkling versus vehicle and increased glycosaminoglycans and procollagen I in biopsies.

references.authors: Weinstock MA, Bingham SF, Digiovanna JJ, et al.
references.title: Tretinoin and the prevention of keratinocyte carcinoma (Basal and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin): a veterans affairs randomized chemoprevention trial.
references.finding: VATTC: high-dose topical tretinoin 0.1% for 1.5-5.5 years did not reduce basal-cell (53% vs 54% at 5 years) or squamous-cell carcinoma (28% vs 31%) or actinic keratoses in high-risk veterans.

references.authors: Weinstock MA, Bingham SF, Lew RA, et al.
references.title: Topical tretinoin therapy and all-cause mortality.
references.finding: The VATTC trial was stopped 6 months early because of excess deaths in the tretinoin group; the difference persisted after adjustment, but the investigators judged a causal effect unlikely.

references.authors: Loureiro KD, Kao KK, Jones KL, et al.
references.title: Minor malformations characteristic of the retinoic acid embryopathy and other birth outcomes in children of women exposed to topical tretinoin during early pregnancy.
references.finding: First-trimester exposure to topical tretinoin was not associated with more miscarriage, major birth defects, or the minor malformations typical of retinoic-acid embryopathy.

references.authors: Middelkamp-Hup MA, Pathak MA, Parrado C, et al.
references.title: Oral Polypodium leucotomos extract decreases ultraviolet-induced damage of human skin.
references.finding: A single oral dose of Polypodium leucotomos extract (7.5 mg/kg) reduced UV erythema, sunburn cells, cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and mast-cell infiltration in irradiated skin (uncontrolled within-person design).

references.authors: Zundell MP, Katz A, Shah M, et al.
references.title: The Utility of Oral Polypodium Leucotomos Extract for Dermatologic Diseases: A Systematic Review.
references.finding: Systematic review of oral Polypodium leucotomos extract across photoaging/skin cancer, actinic keratosis, photodermatoses, melasma, vitiligo and atopic dermatitis: promising photoprotective signals and good safety, from small studies.

references.authors: Stahl W, Heinrich U, Wiseman S, et al.
references.title: Dietary tomato paste protects against ultraviolet light-induced erythema in humans.
references.finding: 40 g/day tomato paste (~16 mg lycopene) with olive oil for 10 weeks reduced UV-induced erythema by 40% versus olive oil alone; no effect was seen at 4 weeks.

references.authors: Rizwan M, Rodriguez-Blanco I, Harbottle A, et al.
references.title: Tomato paste rich in lycopene protects against cutaneous photodamage in humans in vivo: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: 55 g/day tomato paste (16 mg lycopene) for 12 weeks raised the erythema threshold (D30) and reduced UV-induced MMP-1 and mitochondrial DNA damage versus olive oil alone.

references.authors: Köpcke W, Krutmann J
references.title: Protection from sunburn with beta-Carotene--a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Beta-carotene supplements protected against sunburn, but only after at least 10 weeks, with protection growing about 0.5 SD per extra month.

references.authors: Zhang X, Zhou Q, Qi Y, et al.
references.title: The effect of tomato and lycopene on clinical characteristics and molecular markers of UV-induced skin deterioration: A systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention trials.
references.finding: Tomato and lycopene supplementation reduced UV erythema, MMP-1 and pigmentation and raised the minimal erythema dose in healthy people.

references.authors: Hercberg S, Ezzedine K, Guinot C, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplementation increases the risk of skin cancers in women but not in men.
references.finding: SU.VI.MAX: a nutritional-dose antioxidant capsule (vitamin C, E, beta-carotene, selenium, zinc) for 7.5 years raised skin-cancer incidence in women (HR 1.68) and melanoma (HR 4.31, few cases), with no significant effect in men.

references.authors: Guyuron B, Rowe DJ, Weinfeld AB, et al.
references.title: Factors contributing to the facial aging of identical twins.
references.finding: Within identical twin pairs, longer smoking, more sun exposure and lack of sunscreen were associated with an older appearance; heavier weight looked older before 40 but younger after 40.

references.authors: Okada HC, Alleyne B, Varghai K, et al.
references.title: Facial changes caused by smoking: a comparison between smoking and nonsmoking identical twins.
references.finding: Smoking twins had worse upper-eyelid redundancy, lower-lid and malar bags, nasolabial folds, lip wrinkles and jowls than their non-smoking identical twins.

references.authors: Goodman GD, Kaufman J, Day D, et al.
references.title: Impact of Smoking and Alcohol Use on Facial Aging in Women: Results of a Large Multinational, Multiracial, Cross-sectional Survey.
references.finding: In a multinational self-rated survey, smoking was linked to worse forehead, crow's-feet and glabellar lines and other features, and heavy alcohol use to more severe under-eye puffiness, oral commissures, midface volume loss and blood vessels (funded by Allergan).

references.authors: Oyetakin-White P, Suggs A, Koo B, et al.
references.title: Does poor sleep quality affect skin ageing?
references.finding: Poor sleepers had higher intrinsic skin-aging scores, worse skin-barrier recovery (good sleepers recovered 30% better at 72 h) and slower recovery from UV erythema than good sleepers.

references.authors: Sundelin T, Lekander M, Kecklund G, et al.
references.title: Cues of fatigue: effects of sleep deprivation on facial appearance.
references.finding: After 31 hours awake, faces were rated as having more hanging eyelids, darker circles, paler skin and more wrinkles/fine lines than after normal sleep.

references.authors: Vierkötter A, Schikowski T, Ranft U, et al.
references.title: Airborne particle exposure and extrinsic skin aging.
references.finding: Higher traffic-related soot and particle exposure at home was associated with about 20% more pigment spots on the face and, less strongly, more wrinkles.

references.authors: Matta MK, Florian J, Zusterzeel R, et al.
references.title: Effect of Sunscreen Application on Plasma Concentration of Sunscreen Active Ingredients: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: All six common organic sunscreen filters exceeded the FDA 0.5 ng/mL systemic-absorption threshold after a single application; the clinical significance is unknown and the authors did not advise against sunscreen.

references.authors: Passeron T, Bouillon R, Callender V, et al.
references.title: Sunscreen photoprotection and vitamin D status.
references.finding: International expert consensus (including industry scientists): broad-spectrum sunscreens that prevent sunburn are unlikely to compromise vitamin D status in healthy people; at-risk groups should be screened and supplemented.

references.authors: Silva ESD, Tavares R, Paulitsch FDS, et al.
references.title: Use of sunscreen and risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Mostly case-control studies showed no association between sunscreen use and melanoma (OR 1.10) or non-melanoma skin cancer (OR 0.99); early studies' positive associations faded over time.

references.authors: Rueegg CS, Stenehjem JS, Egger M, et al.
references.title: Challenges in assessing the sunscreen-melanoma association.
references.finding: Sunscreen-melanoma associations varied by design; adjusting for sun exposure, sunburn and phenotype consistently moved estimates toward protection, and the RCT showed HR 0.49, while cohort studies showed positive associations likely due to confounding.

references.authors: Cobley JN, Fiorello ML, Bailey DM
references.title: 13 reasons why the brain is susceptible to oxidative stress.
references.finding: The brain uses about 20% of basal oxygen; reasons for its oxidative vulnerability include PUFA-rich membranes, mitochondria, calcium and glutamate signalling, modest antioxidant defences, redox-active metals and neurotransmitter auto-oxidation, with ROS also needed for normal signalling.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: Oxidative stress and neurodegeneration: where are we now?
references.finding: The brain is poorly equipped with antioxidant defences, and oxidative damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation and inflammation are intertwined in neurodegeneration.

references.authors: Butterfield DA, Halliwell B
references.title: Oxidative stress, dysfunctional glucose metabolism and Alzheimer disease.
references.finding: Oxidative damage to glycolytic, TCA-cycle and ATP-synthase enzymes plausibly contributes to the sharp fall in brain glucose metabolism seen in Alzheimer disease and amnestic MCI.

references.authors: Nunomura A, Perry G, Aliev G, et al.
references.title: Oxidative damage is the earliest event in Alzheimer disease.
references.finding: Neuronal RNA oxidation (8-OHG) and nitrotyrosine were greatest early in Alzheimer disease and declined as amyloid deposition increased, suggesting oxidative damage precedes plaques and tangles.

references.authors: Sano M, Ernesto C, Thomas RG, et al.
references.title: A controlled trial of selegiline, alpha-tocopherol, or both as treatment for Alzheimer's disease. The Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study.
references.finding: Unadjusted outcomes were null; after adjusting for baseline MMSE imbalance, 2000 IU/day vitamin E delayed the composite end point (670 vs 440 days).

references.authors: Petersen RC, Thomas RG, Grundman M, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E and donepezil for the treatment of mild cognitive impairment.
references.finding: 2000 IU/day vitamin E for 3 years did not slow progression from MCI to Alzheimer disease (HR 1.02), including in APOE4 carriers.

references.authors: Dysken MW, Sano M, Asthana S, et al.
references.title: Effect of vitamin E and memantine on functional decline in Alzheimer disease: the TEAM-AD VA cooperative randomized trial.
references.finding: TEAM-AD: 2000 IU/day alpha-tocopherol slowed functional decline by 3.15 ADCS-ADL points (about 19% per year, ~6 months' delay) versus placebo over 2.3 years; memantine and the combination did not.

references.authors: Farina N, Llewellyn D, Isaac MGEKN, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E for Alzheimer's dementia and mild cognitive impairment.
references.finding: Cochrane: no evidence of clinically important cognitive benefit of vitamin E in AD or of preventing progression from MCI; moderate-quality evidence suggests possible slowing of functional decline in AD and no increase in serious adverse events.

references.authors: Kryscio RJ, Abner EL, Caban-Holt A, et al.
references.title: Association of Antioxidant Supplement Use and Dementia in the Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease by Vitamin E and Selenium Trial (PREADViSE).
references.finding: PREADViSE (within SELECT): vitamin E (400 IU/day) or selenium (200 ug/day) did not prevent dementia (HRs 0.88 and 0.83, non-significant).

references.authors: Galasko DR, Peskind E, Clark CM, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants for Alzheimer disease: a randomized clinical trial with cerebrospinal fluid biomarker measures.
references.finding: Vitamin E + C + alpha-lipoic acid lowered CSF F2-isoprostanes by 19% but did not change amyloid or tau and was associated with faster MMSE decline.

references.authors: Parkinson Study Group QE3 Investigators, Beal MF, Oakes D, et al.
references.title: A randomized clinical trial of high-dosage coenzyme Q10 in early Parkinson disease: no evidence of benefit.
references.finding: QE3: CoQ10 1200 or 2400 mg/day was stopped for futility, with slight adverse trends versus placebo (UPDRS worsening 7.5 and 8.0 vs 6.9 points).

references.authors: Shults CW, Oakes D, Kieburtz K, et al.
references.title: Effects of coenzyme Q10 in early Parkinson disease: evidence of slowing of the functional decline.
references.finding: The pilot trial suggested CoQ10 1200 mg/day slowed functional decline (UPDRS +6.7 vs +12.0 on placebo), the result QE3 later failed to confirm.

references.authors: Parkinson Study Group
references.title: Effects of tocopherol and deprenyl on the progression of disability in early Parkinson's disease.
references.finding: DATATOP: 2000 IU/day tocopherol did not delay disability in early Parkinson's disease, whereas deprenyl did.

references.authors: Parkinson Study Group SURE-PD3 Investigators, Schwarzschild MA, Ascherio A, et al.
references.title: Effect of Urate-Elevating Inosine on Early Parkinson Disease Progression: The SURE-PD3 Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: SURE-PD3: raising serum urate (an endogenous antioxidant) by 44% with inosine did not slow Parkinson's progression and increased kidney stones; the trial stopped for futility.

references.authors: Devos D, Labreuche J, Rascol O, et al.
references.title: Trial of Deferiprone in Parkinson's Disease.
references.finding: FAIRPARK-II: the iron chelator deferiprone lowered nigrostriatal iron but worsened parkinsonism (MDS-UPDRS +15.6 vs +6.3 points over 36 weeks).

references.authors: Ayton S, Barton D, Brew B, et al.
references.title: Deferiprone in Alzheimer Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.n: 81 people with MCI or early Alzheimer disease
references.finding: Deferiprone lowered hippocampal iron but accelerated cognitive decline, mainly executive function, versus placebo.

references.authors: Kang JH, Cook NR, Manson JE, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E, vitamin C, beta carotene, and cognitive function among women with or at risk of cardiovascular disease: The Women's Antioxidant and Cardiovascular Study.
references.finding: WACS cognitive substudy: vitamin E and beta-carotene did not slow cognitive change over 5.4 years; vitamin C gave inconsistent results.

references.authors: Grodstein F, Kang JH, Glynn RJ, et al.
references.title: A randomized trial of beta carotene supplementation and cognitive function in men: the Physicians' Health Study II.
references.finding: PHS II: short-term beta-carotene had no cognitive effect, but men randomized for about 18 years scored slightly higher on global cognition (0.047 SD) and verbal memory.

references.authors: Baker LD, Manson JE, Rapp SR, et al.
references.title: Effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function: A randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: COSMOS-Mind: cocoa extract (500 mg flavanols/day) had no effect on global cognition over 3 years, while a daily multivitamin gave a small benefit (0.07 SD), most in people with cardiovascular disease.

references.authors: Yeung LK, Alschuler DM, Wall M, et al.
references.title: Multivitamin Supplementation Improves Memory in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: COSMOS-Web: a daily multivitamin improved immediate word-list recall at 1 year and over 3 years, estimated as equivalent to 3.1 years of age-related memory change; secondary outcomes were null.

references.authors: Vyas CM, Manson JE, Sesso HD, et al.
references.title: Effect of multivitamin-mineral supplementation versus placebo on cognitive function: results from the clinic subcohort of the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial and meta-analysis of 3 cognitive studies within COSMOS.
references.finding: COSMOS-Clinic showed a borderline multivitamin benefit on global cognition and a significant episodic-memory benefit; pooling the three COSMOS substudies gave 0.07 SD for global cognition, framed as about 2 years less cognitive aging.

references.authors: Vyas CM, Manson JE, Sesso HD, et al.
references.title: Effect of cocoa extract supplementation on cognitive function: results from the clinic subcohort of the COSMOS trial.
references.finding: COSMOS-Clinic: cocoa extract had no effect on 2-year global or domain-specific cognition; uncorrected subgroup analyses hinted at benefit in people with poorer diet quality.

references.authors: Brickman AM, Yeung LK, Alschuler DM, et al.
references.title: Dietary flavanols restore hippocampal-dependent memory in older adults with lower diet quality and lower habitual flavanol consumption.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: COSMOS-Web flavanol substudy: no memory benefit overall at 1 year (primary end point null), but improvement among people with lower habitual diet quality or flavanol intake; two authors were Mars employees.

references.authors: Brickman AM, Khan UA, Provenzano FA, et al.
references.title: Enhancing dentate gyrus function with dietary flavanols improves cognition in older adults.
references.finding: A 3-month high-cocoa-flavanol drink improved dentate-gyrus function on fMRI and a matched memory task versus a low-flavanol drink (small, Mars-supported).

references.authors: Sachs BC, Williams BJ, Gaussoin SA, et al.
references.title: Impact of multivitamin-mineral and cocoa extract on incidence of mild cognitive impairment and dementia: Results from the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study for the Mind (COSMOS-Mind).
references.finding: COSMOS-Mind: neither multivitamin nor cocoa extract reduced incident MCI or dementia over 3 years (110 MCI and 14 dementia cases; low power).

references.authors: Grodstein F, O'Brien J, Kang JH, et al.
references.title: Long-term multivitamin supplementation and cognitive function in men: a randomized trial.
references.finding: PHS II: a daily multivitamin for about 12 years did not change cognitive decline or verbal memory (global difference -0.01 SD).

references.authors: Barnes LL, Dhana K, Liu X, et al.
references.title: Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons.
references.n: 604 adults 65+ with family history of dementia
references.finding: The 3-year MIND trial: global cognition improved similarly with the MIND diet and a control diet, both with mild caloric restriction (difference 0.035 SD, P=0.23); MRI outcomes did not differ.

references.authors: Morris MC, Tangney CC, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: MIND diet associated with reduced incidence of Alzheimer's disease.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest tertile of MIND-diet score was associated with 53% lower Alzheimer incidence (HR 0.47); moderate adherence was associated with 35% lower risk.

references.authors: Glans I, Sonestedt E, Nägga K, et al.
references.title: Association Between Dietary Habits in Midlife With Dementia Incidence Over a 20-Year Period.
references.finding: Over 20 years, midlife adherence to conventional dietary guidelines or a modified Mediterranean diet was not associated with dementia, Alzheimer disease or amyloid accumulation.

references.authors: Hosking DE, Eramudugolla R, Cherbuin N, et al.
references.title: MIND not Mediterranean diet related to 12-year incidence of cognitive impairment in an Australian longitudinal cohort study.
references.finding: MIND-diet adherence, but not Mediterranean-diet adherence, was associated with lower 12-year odds of cognitive impairment (OR 0.47).

references.authors: Valls-Pedret C, Sala-Vila A, Serra-Mir M, et al.
references.title: Mediterranean Diet and Age-Related Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: PREDIMED-Barcelona substudy: Mediterranean diet plus olive oil or nuts improved memory or frontal composites versus a low-fat control diet over about 4 years, in which cognition declined.

references.authors: Krikorian R, Shidler MD, Nash TA, et al.
references.title: Blueberry supplementation improves memory in older adults.
references.finding: Wild blueberry juice for 12 weeks improved paired-associate learning and word-list recall in a tiny uncontrolled pilot with early memory changes.

references.authors: Miller MG, Hamilton DA, Joseph JA, et al.
references.title: Dietary blueberry improves cognition among older adults in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
references.finding: Freeze-dried blueberry (24 g/day, equivalent to 1 cup fresh) for 90 days reduced repetition errors in verbal learning and task-switching cost versus placebo, with no gait or balance benefit.

references.authors: Cheatham CL, Canipe LG 3rd, Millsap G, et al.
references.title: Six-month intervention with wild blueberries improved speed of processing in mild cognitive decline: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial.
references.n: older adults with mild cognitive decline
references.finding: Six months of wild blueberry powder improved speed of processing versus placebo on CANTAB and ERP measures.

references.authors: Devore EE, Kang JH, Breteler MM, et al.
references.title: Dietary intakes of berries and flavonoids in relation to cognitive decline.
references.finding: Higher blueberry and strawberry intake was associated with slower cognitive decline, equivalent to up to 2.5 years of delayed cognitive aging.

references.authors: He Y, Yang J, Zhang S, et al.
references.title: Blueberry consumption enhances vascular function but not cognitive abilities in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Blueberry interventions improved flow-mediated dilation by 1.11% but did not significantly improve executive function, mood or blood pressure.

references.authors: da Silva ABN, de Oliveira GM, Gallo Ruelas M, et al.
references.title: Blueberries for brainpower: A systematic review and meta-analysis with Bayesian post hoc analysis of RCTS exploring cognitive function in the elderly with prior cognitive decline.
references.finding: In older adults with MCI or subjective decline, chronic blueberry intake improved episodic memory (SMD 0.34) but not processing speed, recognition, visuospatial or working memory.

references.authors: Burckhardt M, Herke M, Wustmann T, et al.
references.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the treatment of dementia.
references.finding: Cochrane: omega-3 supplements had no effect on cognition, daily activities or dementia severity (high-quality evidence).

references.authors: Chew EY, Clemons TE, Agrón E, et al.
references.title: Effect of Omega-3 Fatty Acids, Lutein/Zeaxanthin, or Other Nutrient Supplementation on Cognitive Function: The AREDS2 Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: AREDS2: 1 g/day omega-3 (or lutein/zeaxanthin) for 5 years did not change cognitive decline.

references.authors: Quinn JF, Raman R, Thomas RG, et al.
references.title: Docosahexaenoic acid supplementation and cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease: a randomized trial.
references.finding: DHA 2 g/day for 18 months did not slow cognitive or functional decline or brain atrophy.

references.authors: Kang JH, Vyas CM, Okereke OI, et al.
references.title: Marine n-3 fatty acids and cognitive change among older adults in the VITAL randomized trial.
references.finding: 1 g/day marine omega-3 for 2-3 years did not affect cognitive change (pooled difference -0.01 SD/year).

references.authors: Zhang Y, Chen J, Qiu J, et al.
references.title: Intakes of fish and polyunsaturated fatty acids and mild-to-severe cognitive impairment risks: a dose-response meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies.
references.finding: Each extra weekly serving of fish was associated with 5% lower dementia and 7% lower Alzheimer risk, and each 0.1 g/day dietary DHA with 14% lower dementia risk, with high heterogeneity.

references.authors: Yassine HN, Braskie MN, Mack WJ, et al.
references.title: Association of Docosahexaenoic Acid Supplementation With Alzheimer Disease Stage in Apolipoprotein E ε4 Carriers: A Review.
references.finding: Mixed omega-3 trial results may reflect APOE4 genotype and disease stage: trials in symptomatic AD are negative, while predementia and APOE4-specific effects remain plausible but unproven.

references.authors: Andrieu S, Guyonnet S, Coley N, et al.
references.title: Effect of long-term omega 3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation with or without multidomain intervention on cognitive function in elderly adults with memory complaints (MAPT): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
references.n: 1680 older adults with memory complaints or frailty
references.finding: MAPT: 3 years of omega-3 (800 mg DHA + 225 mg EPA/day), with or without a multidomain intervention, did not significantly slow cognitive decline.

references.authors: Smith AD, Smith SM, de Jager CA, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine-lowering by B vitamins slows the rate of accelerated brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: VITACOG: folic acid 0.8 mg, B6 20 mg and B12 0.5 mg daily for 2 years slowed brain atrophy (0.76% vs 1.08%/year) and by 53% in those with homocysteine above 13 umol/L.

references.authors: de Jager CA, Oulhaj A, Jacoby R, et al.
references.title: Cognitive and clinical outcomes of homocysteine-lowering B-vitamin treatment in mild cognitive impairment: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: B vitamins lowered homocysteine 30% and stabilized executive function; global cognition, memory and clinical ratings benefited only when baseline homocysteine was above the median (11.3 umol/L).

references.authors: Douaud G, Refsum H, de Jager CA, et al.
references.title: Preventing Alzheimer's disease-related gray matter atrophy by B-vitamin treatment.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: B vitamins reduced atrophy up to seven-fold in Alzheimer-vulnerable grey-matter regions, with benefit confined to those with high baseline homocysteine.

references.authors: Oulhaj A, Jernerén F, Refsum H, et al.
references.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acid Status Enhances the Prevention of Cognitive Decline by B Vitamins in Mild Cognitive Impairment.
references.finding: Post hoc VITACOG analysis: B-vitamin effects on memory, global cognition and dementia rating increased with baseline plasma omega-3 levels; no benefit in those with low omega-3.

references.authors: Jernerén F, Elshorbagy AK, Oulhaj A, et al.
references.title: Brain atrophy in cognitively impaired elderly: the importance of long-chain ω-3 fatty acids and B vitamin status in a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: B vitamins slowed atrophy by 40% in those with high baseline omega-3 (>590 umol/L) but not in those with low omega-3 (<390 umol/L).

references.authors: Clarke R, Bennett D, Parish S, et al.
references.title: Effects of homocysteine lowering with B vitamins on cognitive aging: meta-analysis of 11 trials with cognitive data on 22,000 individuals.
references.finding: Lowering homocysteine by about 25% with B vitamins had no effect on global or domain-specific cognitive aging, excluding benefits larger than 1 month per year.

references.authors: Aisen PS, Schneider LS, Sano M, et al.
references.title: High-dose B vitamin supplementation and cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: High-dose B vitamins (folate 5 mg, B6 25 mg, B12 1 mg) lowered homocysteine but did not slow cognitive decline over 18 months; depression adverse events were more frequent.

references.authors: Smith AD, Refsum H, Bottiglieri T, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine and Dementia: An International Consensus Statement.
references.finding: International consensus (Bradford Hill criteria): elevated plasma homocysteine is a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline, dementia and Alzheimer disease in older people.

references.authors: Erickson KI, Voss MW, Prakash RS, et al.
references.title: Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: One year of walking-based aerobic training increased anterior hippocampal volume by 2% (reversing 1-2 years of age-related loss) and improved spatial memory, whereas stretching controls lost volume.

references.authors: Lamb SE, Sheehan B, Atherton N, et al.
references.title: Dementia And Physical Activity (DAPA) trial of moderate to high intensity exercise training for people with dementia: randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: DAPA: 4 months of moderate-high intensity aerobic and strength training improved fitness but slightly worsened cognition at 12 months (ADAS-cog difference -1.4).

references.authors: Firth J, Stubbs B, Vancampfort D, et al.
references.title: Effect of aerobic exercise on hippocampal volume in humans: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Aerobic exercise had no significant effect on total hippocampal volume, but preserved left hippocampal volume by preventing age-related decline.

references.authors: Sink KM, Espeland MA, Castro CM, et al.
references.title: Effect of a 24-Month Physical Activity Intervention vs Health Education on Cognitive Outcomes in Sedentary Older Adults: The LIFE Randomized Trial.
references.finding: LIFE: a 24-month physical activity program did not improve cognition or reduce MCI/dementia versus health education.

references.authors: Xie L, Kang H, Xu Q, et al.
references.title: Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain.
references.finding: In mice, sleep and anesthesia expanded brain interstitial space by 60% and increased clearance of beta-amyloid and other solutes (the glymphatic hypothesis).

references.authors: Shokri-Kojori E, Wang GJ, Wiers CE, et al.
references.title: β-Amyloid accumulation in the human brain after one night of sleep deprivation.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: One night of sleep deprivation increased beta-amyloid PET signal in the right hippocampus and thalamus (crossover design).

references.authors: Eide PK, Vinje V, Pripp AH, et al.
references.title: Sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain.
references.finding: After intrathecal gadobutrol, one night of total sleep deprivation slowed tracer clearance from most brain regions on MRI, without catch-up on the next night's sleep.

references.authors: Miao A, Luo T, Hsieh B, et al.
references.title: Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia.
references.finding: Measuring fluorescent tracers in mouse brains, clearance was reduced, not increased, during sleep and anesthesia, contradicting the glymphatic sleep-clearance model.

references.authors: Sabia S, Fayosse A, Dumurgier J, et al.
references.title: Association of sleep duration in middle and old age with incidence of dementia.
references.finding: Sleeping 6 hours or less at age 50-60 was associated with 22-37% higher dementia risk over 25 years, and persistent short sleep with about 30% higher risk.

references.authors: Lin FR, Pike JR, Albert MS, et al.
references.title: Hearing intervention versus health education control to reduce cognitive decline in older adults with hearing loss in the USA (ACHIEVE): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: ACHIEVE: hearing aids plus audiology did not slow 3-year cognitive decline overall (difference 0.002 SD); a prespecified sensitivity analysis suggested benefit in the higher-risk ARIC cohort but not the healthier de novo cohort.

references.authors: Livingston G, Huntley J, Liu KY, et al.
references.title: Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission.
references.finding: Lancet Commission 2024: 14 potentially modifiable risk factors (adding high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss to the 2020 list) account for about 45% of dementia cases worldwide.

references.authors: Wilker EH, Osman M, Weisskopf MG
references.title: Ambient air pollution and clinical dementia: systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Each 2 ug/m3 of PM2.5 was associated with a dementia HR of 1.04 (0.99-1.09) overall and 1.42 in studies with active case finding; NO2 and NOx associations were weaker and ozone showed none.

references.authors: Block ML, Calderón-Garcidueñas L
references.title: Air pollution: mechanisms of neuroinflammation and CNS disease.
references.finding: Air pollution components reach the brain directly and via systemic inflammation, activating microglia and damaging the blood-brain barrier, a chronic source of ROS and neuroinflammation.

references.authors: Maher BA, Ahmed IA, Karloukovski V, et al.
references.title: Magnetite pollution nanoparticles in the human brain.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Abundant rounded magnetite nanoparticles in human brain tissue matched combustion-derived airborne pollution particles, a potential redox-active iron source.

references.authors: Daviet R, Aydogan G, Jagannathan K, et al.
references.title: Associations between alcohol consumption and gray and white matter volumes in the UK Biobank.
references.finding: Alcohol intake was associated with lower global brain volume, regional grey matter and white-matter integrity, already at an average of 1-2 units a day, with stronger associations at higher intake.

references.authors: Topiwala A, Wang C, Ebmeier KP, et al.
references.title: Associations between moderate alcohol consumption, brain iron, and cognition in UK Biobank participants: Observational and mendelian randomization analyses.
references.finding: Drinking more than 7 units a week was associated with higher iron in the putamen, caudate and substantia nigra, which was associated with poorer executive function and fluid intelligence; Mendelian randomization evidence was weak.

references.authors: Topiwala A, Allan CL, Valkanova V, et al.
references.title: Moderate alcohol consumption as risk factor for adverse brain outcomes and cognitive decline: longitudinal cohort study.
references.finding: Over 30 years, 14-21 units a week carried 3.4 times the odds of right hippocampal atrophy compared with abstinence, over 30 units 5.8 times, and light drinking showed no protection.

references.authors: Sabia S, Fayosse A, Dumurgier J, et al.
references.title: Alcohol consumption and risk of dementia: 23 year follow-up of Whitehall II cohort study.
references.finding: Both midlife abstinence (HR 1.47) and drinking over 14 units/week (each extra 7 units +17%) were associated with higher dementia risk over 23 years.

references.authors: Topiwala A, Levey DF, Zhou H, et al.
references.title: Alcohol use and risk of dementia in diverse populations: evidence from cohort, case-control and Mendelian randomisation approaches.
references.finding: Observational analyses showed a U-shaped alcohol-dementia curve, but genetic analyses showed a monotonic rise in risk with drinking (OR 1.15 per SD) and suggested reverse causation explains the apparent benefit of light drinking.
